paragraphs: Swamiji urged his listeners to choose one ideal of God, their Ishta, and give their whole soul to it, practising day after day until it grows and fills everything. But, he warned, we must also honour the ideals other people hold. Otherwise devotion turns into fanaticism. To show this, he told an old story.

In India some people worship God as Shiva and others as Vishnu. There was once a man who was utterly devoted to Shiva, and along with that devotion he carried a fierce hatred for anyone who worshipped Vishnu. He could not stand even hearing the name. Since Vishnu's devotees were everywhere, he came up with a plan: he pierced his ears and hung two little bells from them. Whenever someone said 'Vishnu', he shook his head and the jingling drowned out the word.
Then Shiva himself appeared to him in a dream and scolded him. Shiva and Vishnu were the same; there were not two Gods, only two names. The man did not care. He wanted nothing to do with Vishnu.

He kept a small image of Shiva on a beautiful altar. One day he brought home some lovely incense and lit it before his God. As the smoke curled up, he saw the image split into two: one half was still Shiva, and the other half had become Vishnu. At once he leaped up and pressed his finger under the Vishnu half's nostril, so it could not enjoy even a whiff of his incense.

At that, Shiva was disgusted, and the man was turned into a demon. He is the 'bell-eared' one, Ghanta Karna, the father of all fanatics. Swamiji described how Indian boys would worship him with a clay image and the foulest-smelling forest flowers, and then beat the image with sticks. That is the fitting honour, he suggested, for the patron of everyone who hates every god but their own.
learn: Being committed to your own beliefs and respecting other people's are not opposites. Strong conviction becomes ugly when it shuts its ears to everyone else. Hold your path firmly, and let others walk theirs.
